name: Global cross-country learning for monthly physical petroleum-import forecasting in landlocked economies
strongest_existing_work: Montero-Manso and Hyndman (2021); Hewamalage et al. (2022b); Semenoglou et al. (2021); Baltagi and Griffin (1997); Zhu (2023); Yolusever (2026); Laborda et al. (2023)
what_is_achieved: Theory and benchmarks show global models are not more restrictive than local ones and often win on related series (Montero-Manso & Hyndman, 2021; Hewamalage et al., 2022b). Pooling across countries for fuel demand has a long history in econometrics (Baltagi and Griffin (1997) compare pooled and heterogeneous estimators for dynamic gasoline demand; abstract not available, findings not extracted). Recent work pools short cross-country panels: a TFT for 25 OECD GDPs (Laborda et al., 2023) and partial pooling on short annual panels, whose gain reverses under strong heterogeneity (Yolusever, 2026).
what_remains: Every petroleum-import forecasting study found is single-country (Indonesia, Taiwan, Thailand, China, India, Tanzania, Nepal) and almost all use values, annual data or demand rather than monthly physical import volumes. No study pools landlocked importers.
search_evidence: First OpenAlex Boolean run: 'landlocked AND (oil OR petroleum OR fuel) AND forecast*' returned 12 records in total, none on target; 'fuel/petroleum AND import* AND forecast* AND (panel OR cross-country OR global model)' returned 30, none forecasting physical imports across countries. Local Boolean check on the 5,230-record pool plus Crossref top 200: 11 and 41 matches, none on target.
novelty_verdict: Application-level novelty, not methodological: pooling is established; the new element is the target (monthly physical refined-product imports) and the landlocked panel.
data_feasibility: Feasible: 44 series in 22 countries (5,549 observations); Tier-1 evaluation set of 22 series. Weak co-movement (median year-on-year correlation near zero) limits the expected pooling gain.
proposed_experiment: Local (ETS/SARIMA, per-series LightGBM) vs global (pooled LightGBM, small GRU/N-BEATS) vs partially pooled (validation-shrunk) models; rolling origin; MASE and pinball loss; leave-one-country-out transfer; HLN-corrected DM tests with Holm adjustment.
rationale: Well-defined and testable; the result may be null because of heterogeneity, which is still publishable if reported honestly.

name: Deep learning versus gradient boosting under comparable data, horizons and evaluation
strongest_existing_work: Januschowski et al. (2022); Makridakis et al. (2022a); Makridakis et al. (2022c); Elsayed et al. (2021); Grinsztajn et al. (2022); Champahom et al. (2025); Shahab et al. (2026); Chinn et al. (2026)
what_is_achieved: Extensively compared in general forecasting: tree-based global models dominated M5 (Januschowski et al., 2022); DL combinations win on some M3 subsets at high cost (Makridakis et al., 2022c); window-based GBRT matches many DL models (Elsayed et al., 2021); trees beat DL on medium tabular data (Grinsztajn et al., 2022). In energy and trade, boosting usually wins on small data: XGBoost over LSTM for Thai transport energy (Champahom et al., 2025) and CatBoost best for bilateral trade (Shahab et al., 2026).
what_remains: No controlled comparison on monthly physical fuel imports with identical information sets, horizons, rolling origins and probabilistic scores.
search_evidence: First OpenAlex run: 36 records for (boosting AND deep learning AND trade/import AND forecast) and 49 for (boosting AND deep learning AND oil/fuel AND demand AND forecast); local check: 108 matches, dominated by electricity, price and building-energy studies.
novelty_verdict: Incremental. The direction of the result is predictable from prior evidence (boosting is likely to win); the value lies in shock-period stratification and calibration.
data_feasibility: Feasible with small models (16-64 hidden units). Neural models are expected to be data-limited.
proposed_experiment: Same features and windows for LightGBM (quantile objective) and GRU/TCN/N-BEATS; stratify errors by normal vs shock windows; report compute cost.
rationale: Necessary benchmark inside the thesis but weak as a headline claim.

name: Calibrated probabilistic forecasting of petroleum imports
strongest_existing_work: Gneiting et al. (2007); Gneiting and Raftery (2007); Hong et al. (2016); Makridakis et al. (2022b); Jensen et al. (2024); Romano et al. (2019); Salim (2026)
what_is_achieved: Probabilistic forecasting and calibration theory are mature (Gneiting et al., 2007; Gneiting & Raftery, 2007); electricity and retail have standard quantile benchmarks (Hong et al., 2016; Makridakis et al., 2022b); conformal wrappers give distribution-free intervals (Romano et al., 2019; Jensen et al., 2024). A 2026 preprint applies quantile regression to aviation-fuel demand for inventory planning (Salim, 2026).
what_remains: Every petroleum-import and national fuel-demand forecasting study found reports point forecasts only (MAPE, RMSE, 'accuracy'). Interval coverage and calibration under shocks are not evaluated.
search_evidence: Local Boolean check (probabilistic terms AND fuel AND import/demand AND forecast): 15 matches; on-target only the aviation-fuel quantile preprint and ship-fuel interval prediction (engineering), none for national imports.
novelty_verdict: Genuine domain gap; methods are existing. Defensible as 'first calibrated probabilistic benchmark' for this target, not as a new method.
data_feasibility: Feasible: quantile LightGBM, conformalised intervals, likelihood-based GRU. Short test windows make coverage estimates noisy, so report confidence bands on coverage.
proposed_experiment: Compare pinball loss/CRPS, 80% and 95% coverage and interval width across models; PIT histograms; conformal recalibration; stratify by shock windows.
rationale: Strong combination of clear gap, direct policy use (risk bands), and standard evaluation tools.

name: Publication-delay-aware (as-of) evaluation of trade-based fuel forecasts
strongest_existing_work: Stark and Croushore (2002); Baumeister and Kilian (2011); Chinn et al. (2026); Agyekum and Obese (2026); Intarasat et al. (2026); Briggs (2025); Martin and Swanson (2009)
what_is_achieved: Real-time data are a mature topic in macroeconomics (Stark & Croushore, 2002; Croushore, 2006) and oil-price forecasting, with monthly real-time vintages for 1991-2010 (Baumeister & Kilian, 2011). World-trade nowcasting is evaluated on real-time datasets (Chinn et al., 2026), and ML gains in inflation forecasting have been re-tested on vintages (Agyekum & Obese, 2026). A 2026 preprint masks inputs by release calendar for oil-export nowcasting in Norway and Thailand (Intarasat et al., 2026).
what_remains: No study found forecasts commodity-level imports from UN Comtrade while respecting reporter-specific release dates, which range from about 2 to more than 6 months in the project's panel. Comtrade does not publish full vintage histories, so revisions can only be measured from repeated snapshots.
search_evidence: Local Boolean check (real-time/vintage/publication-lag terms AND trade/oil AND forecast/nowcast): 20 matches; on-target only the macro, oil-price, world-trade and oil-export works listed.
novelty_verdict: Moderately novel in this domain: established concept, new application to reporter-specific trade-data release lags. Strong methodological hygiene contribution.
data_feasibility: Partly feasible: release dates exist (availability endpoint, first-seen dates); true vintages do not, so the design is 'as-of availability' plus snapshot-based revision checks, not full real-time replication.
proposed_experiment: Train/evaluate twice: (i) using latest data with oracle availability, (ii) as-of release dates; report the accuracy gap by horizon; repeat for 2025-2026 first-release vs later snapshots.
rationale: Directly affects whether a warning would have been available in time; data limits must be stated.

name: Incremental forecasting value of supplier concentration, oil prices and geopolitical risk
strongest_existing_work: Caldara and Iacoviello (2022); Huang et al. (2025); Peng et al. (2025); Lin and Zhang (2025); Kwon and Jeong (2026); Cohen et al. (2011); Delis et al. (2025)
what_is_achieved: GPR is a standard index (Caldara & Iacoviello, 2022) and has explanatory links with energy imports and the survival of energy-import relationships (Lin & Zhang, 2025; Peng et al., 2025). GPR's contribution to crude-oil volatility forecasts has been tested (Delis et al., 2025). Kwon and Jeong (2026) show, out of sample, that dynamic trade-flow indicators outperform origin concentration for disruption warnings in Korea.
what_remains: Out-of-sample incremental value of HHI, prices and GPR for fuel-import volume forecasts is untested; most GPR-import studies are explanatory (VAR, survival) rather than predictive. Global GPR barely varies across small landlocked importers, and Kyrgyz shocks (Russian export bans) are not GPR events.
search_evidence: Local Boolean check (GPR/HHI/concentration AND import AND forecast/predict): 29 matches, of which on target are price-volatility forecasting with GPR and Kwon & Jeong's concentration benchmark.
novelty_verdict: Incremental; partially addressed by Kwon & Jeong for product-level imports in a maritime economy. A null result is plausible.
data_feasibility: Feasible as an ablation. Requires publication-lagged features to avoid leakage; supplier shares come from the same lagged Comtrade data.
proposed_experiment: Feature-group ablation (own history; + supplier HHI and shares; + Brent; + GPR; + event dummies) with pinball-loss differences and DM tests per group.
rationale: Cheap to test and informative even if null; should not be the headline.

name: From probabilistic import forecasts to early warning of supply stress
strongest_existing_work: Kwon and Jeong (2026); Yokuş (2024); Khan and Wyrwa (2025); Wang et al. (2018b); Yildirim and Sanyal (2022); Do et al. (2024); Islam et al. (2021)
what_is_achieved: Kwon and Jeong (2026) already define disruption onsets as a persistent quantity shortfall with rising unit values and evaluate warnings out of sample against concentration screening. Energy-crisis warnings exist at world level (Yokuş, 2024) and as index systems (Wang et al., 2018b); renewable-shortfall alarms use boosted forecasts plus a probabilistic classifier with PR-AUC and Brier scores (Khan & Wyrwa, 2025).
what_remains: No study turns calibrated, lag-aware forecasts of refined-fuel imports into warnings for landlocked importers, or checks warnings against documented fuel-supply events. Import shortfalls are proxies; actual retail shortages are rarely observed (one exception: crowdsourced station data in hurricane studies (Islam et al., 2021)).
search_evidence: Local Boolean check (early warning/alarm AND fuel/oil/energy/import AND supply/shortage/disruption/security): 21 matches; closest are those listed.
novelty_verdict: Not novel as a concept; an extension of Kwon & Jeong to refined fuels, landlocked importers and probabilistic forecasts. Must cite that work as the nearest prior study.
data_feasibility: Weakest part: few documented events (2023-2026 Russian restrictions; mid-2026 Kyrgyz shortage), proxy labels, and recent data that are provisional.
proposed_experiment: Define stress as P(import < q-threshold of expected level) using the predictive distribution; compare PR-AUC, recall at a fixed alert budget and lead time with HHI ranking and a quantity-only rule; validate against a sourced event list.
rationale: High practical value; claims must be framed as import-supply stress, not domestic shortage.

name: Landlocked economies as a distinct group in energy-import research
strongest_existing_work: Athukorala and Hill (2023); Kosowska and Kosowski (2022); Akhmetov (2015); Pradhan et al. (2023); Chupilkin et al. (2023); Veselinović and Radukić (2021)
what_is_achieved: Landlocked-country research centres on trade costs, transit and connectivity (World Trade Organization, 2021; Athukorala & Hill, 2023). Central Asian energy security is studied descriptively or with indices (Akhmetov, 2015; Kosowska & Kosowski, 2022). Kyrgyz trade has been reshaped by post-2022 rerouting (Chupilkin et al., 2023).
what_remains: No quantitative forecasting study treats landlocked fuel importers as a group; their fuel imports appear only inside global datasets or single-country studies.
search_evidence: Local Boolean check (landlocked AND energy/fuel AND import/security/dependence): 20 matches, none forecasting fuel imports.
novelty_verdict: Under-explored but mainly a sampling frame; it becomes a scientific contribution only if landlocked-specific mechanisms (corridor dependence, single dominant supplier, transit delays) are shown to matter.
data_feasibility: Feasible, but the panel is heterogeneous (exporters, microstates, transit hubs); Tier-1 restriction reduces it to 13 countries.
proposed_experiment: Compare pooling within the landlocked panel against pooling with a non-landlocked control group of small importers; test whether supplier concentration interacts with landlocked status.
rationale: Useful framing and policy relevance; needs a control group to become a finding.

name: Additional: data-quality-aware forecasting with UN Comtrade (mirror data, revisions, statistical imbalance)
strongest_existing_work: Hu et al. (2022); Golovanova et al. (2026); Briggs (2025); Chupilkin et al. (2023)
what_is_achieved: Statistical imbalance in Comtrade records is widespread, including fossil fuels (Hu et al., 2022); mirror discrepancies surged after 2019 and are affected by sanctions (Golovanova et al., 2026); UN energy statistics are revised (Briggs, 2025).
what_remains: Forecasting studies rarely report how trade-data quality (reporter vs mirror, provisional vs revised) affects accuracy or alert reliability.
search_evidence: Found through the main search and local checks; no forecasting study measuring this effect was found.
novelty_verdict: Moderately novel, practically important, low cost given the project's audit pipeline.
data_feasibility: Feasible: the project already has heading-vs-lines, partner-vs-World and mirror checks.
proposed_experiment: Robustness: re-run evaluation with mirror-based targets and with revision-affected months excluded; report sensitivity of rankings and alerts.
rationale: Strengthens credibility of all other results; good secondary contribution.
